🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is +0.35% (intraday, 7-year -5bp). At trading day 27 (last close) it was +0.41% against a five-campaign average of -1.24% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.84%. The 10-year is -3bp since the hike vs a +16bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 3 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 803bp against a five-year average of 414bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +56bp and BB +42bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.31 → 0.61 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is moving too (+12bp in a month).
  • Bank Earnings: 1 bank reported (BOH); 1 red-flagged (BOH: NPLs +282% QoQ). Credit deteriorating at the margin; deposit costs flat. Watch: BOH.
  • Stocks: Stocks rose about 0.7%, led by tech; Japan fell, Europe and UK gained.
  • FX: Dollar edged up slightly; euro, pound and yen barely moved after hours.
  • Technicals: S&P and Nasdaq sit just under 50-day averages, still well above 200-day.
  • Sectors: Tech and industrials led today; energy, utilities and staples led this month.
  • Credit/Spreads: Most bond risk premiums stay low, but the weakest junk borrowers are under real strain.
  • Crisis: Overall crisis risk looks moderate, mainly from weak junk borrowers and expensive oil.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is steady near 2.6-3%, but energy keeps headline pressure on.
  • Tech Bubble: Prices are far from 2000 extremes, but credit and financial conditions look complacent.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Apple is the biggest name reporting; Flex has the biggest expected move; no IPOs confirmed.
  • Iran: We found no verifiable Iran news from October; the latest confirmed reports are from July.
  • Warsh: We expect Warsh's Fed to hold rates this week, with a lean toward tighter policy.
  • Week Ahead: Fed meeting, mega-cap tech earnings, then job openings and payrolls next week.
  • Outlook: Neutral short term; credit stress and high yields cap the upside.
  • Trades: Upgrade credit quality, buy S&P only above 7,697, avoid gold and comm services.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 sell, 19 hold long, 25 stay out
  • Regime Rules: S&P 500 risk-on; NDX risk-on, 5.1% above its sell trigger; trend intact; credit spreads widening
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.59 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +91bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 90th pctile, +31bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Oil Model: WTI $108.33 (2026-10-23). Oil model Base $107 / $94 / $83 at 3/6/12 months (Bull $99, Bear $67 at 12m), probability-weighted $83, against a futures strip of $99 / $92 / $83. Options imply scenario weights of Base 91%, Bull 0%, Bear 9% (yours 50%/25%/25%). Energy contributes +0.76pp to headline CPI y/y in six months on the weighted path; against flat oil, the oil path itself moves headline CPI by -0.24pp at 6 months and -0.52pp at 12. Demand check: activity data imply +1.4 mb/d y/y against +0.7 from the GDP assumptions — worth a look.
  • Bottom line: Stocks bounced, but the riskiest junk bonds are flashing a warning worth respecting.

Risk assets rallied into the PM close. The S&P 500 rose 0.70% to 7676.77, the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.82% to 26169.38 and the Dow added 0.28%, while the VIX fell 1.06 points to 18.39. Info Tech (+1.5%) and Industrials (+1.4%) led, and Communication Services (-1.42%) kept bleeding. Europe matched the US: the Euro Stoxx 50 rose 0.79% and the FTSE 100 0.72%. The Nikkei fell 0.80%. The bigger story is under the surface of the high-yield market. Headline US HY OAS is calm at 3.37% (computed 25th percentile, z -0.61), but the computed HY contagion panel shows the Caa-B gap at 803bp. That is 64bp wider in a week and 261bp wider in three months, against a 5-year average of about 414bp, which puts it at the 100th percentile of the last 5 years and the widest since 2020-04-15. The FRED ICE CCC-B cross-check agrees: 994bp, also at the 100th 5-year percentile. Is it spreading up the ladder? Partly. Single-B OAS widened 56bp over the month and Ba 42bp, and the 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes rose to 0.61 from 0.31 three months ago. Even so, it is still below its 5-year median of 0.70. The B-Ba gap of 119bp sits at the 50th percentile of its 5-year range, and IG at 89bp is below its 5-year average. So the stress is concentrated at the bottom of the junk market and has lifted single-B and BB levels, but it has not yet broken the relative pricing of B against BB, or IG. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. In rates, the 2-year rose 3.4bp to 4.72% while the 10-year (4.99%) and 30-year (5.30%) slipped, flattening the curve into this week's Fed meeting. Brent at 115.38 keeps an energy-inflation backdrop in place. Sentiment: equity risk appetite recovered, but credit quality is quietly deteriorating.

“The stock market bought the dip today; the CCC market is still selling it, and when those two disagree, the bond market usually has the better memory.”
📊Markets

US equities closed firmly higher: S&P 500 +0.70% (7676.77, +53.09), Nasdaq Comp +0.82% (26169.38), Dow +0.28% (52361.58), Russell 2000 +0.38% (2786.424). Small caps lagged large-cap growth, so this was a mega-cap tech bounce rather than a broad reflation trade. VIX fell 5.45% to 18.39. Europe rallied in sympathy (STOXX 600 +0.77% to 640.66, Euro Stoxx 50 +0.79%, FTSE 100 +0.72% to 10767.33), while the Nikkei 225 fell 0.80% to 62189.65. In rates, the US 2Y rose to 4.7159% (+3.41bp) while the 10Y eased to 4.9884% (-0.61bp) and the 30Y to 5.3028% (-1.93bp), a bear-flattening at the front end ahead of the FOMC. The Bund 10Y rose 2.2bp to 3.367%, and the JGB 10Y (2.801%) and Gilt 10Y (5.344%) dipped. Commodities: WTI 101.76 (chg reported -1.46%), Brent 115.38 (-1.15%), Gold 4012.27 (-0.11%), Silver flat at 53.9652, Copper 654.2 (chg reported +0.53%), Nat Gas 2.602 (chg reported -1.44%). Oil above $100 remains the dominant macro input for inflation and the Fed.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 491.20 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is trading at 491.2 cents/gal, near the top of its historical range on every measure we track: outright price (99.8th percentile, z 3.35), the refining margin (crack at 104.544 $/bbl, 99.7th percentile, z 5.61) and the curve. The futures curve is steeply backwardated, meaning near-month contracts are priced well above later ones: 491.2 in the front month, 376.91 at month 12 and 285.99 at month 36. That points to an acute shortage of prompt barrels, not a lasting repricing of the whole curve. In past episodes when diesel reached readings this high, prices and spreads usually fell back, so four of the five signals point SELL. The only BUY comes from the thin, illiquid far end of the curve.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.59 vol points (21th percentile of the 52 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 102.2 (74th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 86bp (steeper by 11bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (117bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 25 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

Today is far from March 2000 on equity froth, but much closer on the catalyst, regime and signpost conditions. Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (41x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The classic 2000 sequence was extreme valuations, then a late-cycle catalyst (Fed tightening, inverted curve, credit turning), then a bear market. Today the valuation leg is the weakest part of the case: trailing Nasdaq multiples are a fraction of 2000's, and the Nasdaq is only modestly above trend. What looks late-cycle is the financing backdrop. IG and Baa spreads are tighter than at the 2000 peak, conditions are loose, and margin debt is growing 28.8% year over year (40% of the 2000 surge). The CCC-B blowout in the HY contagion panel is the kind of early credit crack that preceded 2000-2002, while sentiment surveys remain cautious rather than euphoric. The analyst-estimate inputs (top-10 concentration about 40%, CAPE about 40x, market cap/GDP about 215%, IPO froth about 30/100, long-term EPS-growth expectations about 65/100) were not re-verified by web search this run and should be treated as approximate. On balance: elevated concentration and aggregate valuation risk, with a dot-com-style mania not confirmed. The dot-com drawdown template (Nasdaq -78% over 31 months from 2000-03-10) is the tail, not the base case.

⚔️Iran War

No Iran-conflict developments dated October 2026 could be verified in this run; search results ended in July. The most recent verifiable report is Just Security's July 22, 2026 Early Edition. It said the US military had carried out its 11th consecutive night of strikes on Iran, and that Iran's army claimed drone attacks on US military facilities in Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain. Earlier in the year, the war widened in early March with US and Israeli strikes on Iran, Iranian retaliation against Gulf targets, and Hezbollah attacks on Israel (KSUT/NPR, 2026-03-02). In May, Iranian officials and the Trump administration gave contradictory assessments of the war and peace talks (Just Security, 2026-05-07). 🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Hold at the October FOMC (inferred). At Warsh's first meeting as chair in June, the Fed held at 3.50-3.75%, its fourth straight pause, and the median projection put year-end fed funds at 3.8%, up from 3.4%. With core PCE at 3.0%, oil above $100 and the 2Y rising 3.4bp today, we infer a hold with a hawkish lean, not a cut. A hike is possible but not our base case. No October-specific market pricing could be verified.

~1 YEAR

Inference: policy rate flat to modestly higher over 12 months, plus a push to shrink the balance sheet and less reliance on forward guidance. Warsh is reported to oppose forward guidance, which implies more meeting-to-meeting volatility in rate expectations. His second press conference was read as dovish, which lowered near-term hike odds, so a deliberate, data-dependent path is more likely than an aggressive one.

Sourced facts: the June 2026 hold at 3.50-3.75% was unanimous, Warsh did not submit a dot, nine of 19 participants saw higher rates by year-end, and the year-end PCE projection was 3.6% (Spectrum News, Kitco, NST). Franklin Templeton characterized the reaction to his second press conference as dovish, with most analysts putting less than even odds on a July hike. SoFi expects decisions to stay data-driven under Warsh. Everything about October and the next year is our inference from those statements plus today's data. We found no direct citation for October 2026 pricing or the September projections.

Sources: Spectrum News - Fed Chair Kevin Warsh first meeting: FOMC expectations · Kitco - Warsh-led Fed expected to hold interest rates steady · Franklin Templeton - On My Mind: Mr. Warsh, how soon is now · Seeking Alpha - Fed rate decisions likely to stay data-driven under Warsh: SoFi · America's Credit Unions - New Fed Chair Warsh and the future of the Fed
